tasks.short: Set up vendor meetings, prepare with failure and usage data, meet, try samples with mechanics and pass choices to purchasing.

steps.what: Vendor representative asks for a meeting: by e-mail today, by booking a slot through the supervisor's calendar link after the change
Supervisor arranges meetings with vendor representatives by e-mail and phone
Supervisor looks up failures, usage and prices of the vendor's products used in repair work
Supervisor meets vendors or suppliers to discuss products and problems
Supervisor tries out sample products with the mechanics
Supervisor writes notes and product choices: in an e-mail today, on the supplier record in the procurement system after the change
Supervisor checks the final notes and product choices: products, trial results and reasons
Supervisor passes the checked product choices to purchasing
Buyer negotiates prices and terms with the supplier

tasks.design: A report in the maintenance management system ({OTHER}) shows per product the parts used, failures coded and prices paid, so the supervisor goes into the meeting with numbers. Vendor reps book through a calendar link. The supervisor writes notes and product choices on the supplier record in the {PROCUREMENT} system, checks them and passes them to purchasing once; the meeting and trials stay as they are.
tasks.previous_blocker: Usage and failure data had to be gathered by hand before each meeting.
tasks.enabler_now: Maintenance systems link parts usage and failure codes to products and suppliers.
tasks.still_hard: Judging whether a new product is better needs trials on real equipment.
tasks.human_edge: Pushing a vendor on a recurring failure and knowing what the mechanics will actually use.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; meetings start from data.

reach.learn: Whether failure data per product strengthens negotiations.

evidence.claim: An enterprise asset management system links maintenance with ERP and supply chain and supports failure-mode strategies.
Calendar booking links and supplier records are standard tools.

assumptions: Boundary: from arranging the meeting to passing choices to purchasing; contract signing is outside.
Input contract: parts usage booked by mechanics on job orders; failure causes coded on closed job orders; prices from purchase orders; fallback is gathering by hand.
Buyer and vendor time is outside the supervisor's savings.

Meetings, trials, writing the notes, the check and passing the choices on keep their full time. s1 keeps 50 because some vendors still phone; s2 keeps 50 for reading the report and adding what it lacks. The vendor's booking is shown in s7.
unknowns: Whether failure causes are coded today.
How many vendor meetings per month.
research_questions: Do data-backed meetings change which products are kept?

incremental.description: No new upkeep: writing product notes on the supplier record is s5, and the vendor's booking is s7.

approvals.approved_version: The notes and product choices exactly as checked by the supervisor in s5c, passed once to the buyer on that supplier's record in the {PROCUREMENT} system; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: failure causes are not coded on job orders, so usage and failures are still gathered by hand (7.2); high: causes coded and usage booked (13.8).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Estimate next year's maintenance budget, agree it, link orders and invoices to jobs, monitor spending and explain overruns.

steps.what: Supervisor estimates next year's maintenance costs per asset group in a spreadsheet
Supervisor discusses the budget preparation with the maintenance manager and controller
Controller consolidates the department budget
Supervisor matches purchasing documentation and invoices to job orders
Supervisor monitors departmental expenditures against budget from monthly exports
Supervisor files quotes, order confirmations and delivery notes
Supervisor explains overruns to the controller

tasks.design: Purchase orders raised from job orders in the maintenance management system ({OTHER}) carry the asset and cost centre into the {ERP}, so invoices land on the right job without matching by hand, and order confirmations arrive on the order; the supervisor still attaches quotes and delivery notes. Last year's actuals per asset group give the budget base, and a {BI} view shows spending against budget each month; the supervisor explains and decides.
tasks.previous_blocker: Costs were coded loosely and rebuilt in spreadsheets from ERP exports.
tasks.enabler_now: Maintenance systems link job orders to ERP purchasing; a documented case moved from partly spreadsheet-based follow-up to such a system.
tasks.still_hard: Budget choices depend on plant plans and asset condition; coding is only right if every order starts from a job.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing which machines will need money next year and arguing for it.

ambition.what: Spending checked against budget every month per asset group instead of at year end.

tasks.altitude: The supervisor reviews variances instead of compiling them; budget decisions stay with the manager and controller.

reach.learn: Whether job-level costs improve budget accuracy.

evidence.claim: An enterprise asset management system links maintenance with ERP and supply chain.
A Belgian lubricants plant saved about EUR 360,000 a year, nearly 20% of its maintenance budget, after moving maintenance follow-up from spreadsheets to such a system (vendor case).
Linking purchase orders to job orders lets invoices post to the right asset and cost centre.

assumptions: Boundary: from budget preparation to explaining variances; approving invoices for payment is outside.

Input contract: asset and cost centre on every job order kept by the maintenance planner; purchase orders raised from job orders by buyers; cost centre structure set by the controller; fallback is the spreadsheet.
Controller and buyer time is outside the supervisor's savings.

Budget talks and overrun explanations keep their full time. s1 keeps 50 because the actuals base is built and the supervisor still estimates; s4 and s5 keep 50 for exceptions and reading the view; s6 keeps 60 because quotes and delivery notes are still attached by hand.
unknowns: Share of purchases raised from job orders today.
research_questions: Do monthly variances per asset group change spending decisions during the year?

already_counted.description: Supervisor checks the budget base built from last year's actuals.
Supervisor clears invoices that did not match a job order.

incremental.description: Supervisor makes sure every order starts from a job order.
Controller keeps the cost mapping and dashboard current.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: many purchases bypass job orders, so invoices are still matched by hand (28.4); high: orders start from job orders (36.8).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Write the scope, request and compare contractor quotes, choose and get approval, coordinate access and safety, and accept the completed work.

steps.what: Supervisor writes the scope of work for the contractor job
Supervisor prepares quote requests for approved contractors: by e-mail today, from the procurement system after the change
Supervisor checks the final quote request: scope, site, dates and the contractors it goes to
Supervisor sends the checked quote request to the selected contractors
Supervisor copies prices, hours, exclusions and lead times from quotes into a spreadsheet

loop.input: Contractor quote documents in different layouts.
loop.output: One row per quote with total price, rates, hours, materials, exclusions and lead time, each with the quoted text it came from.
loop.check: Every value must show its source text and line items must add up to the stated total. A second check compares each value with its source text (the quoted text states that price, hours or lead time for that line) and each exclusion with the scope; any value the text does not support, and any unclear value, stays blank for the supervisor.
loop.stop: One pass per quote; unreadable quotes go to the supervisor.
loop.why_not_simpler: Each contractor uses its own layout and wording; a fixed template cannot read them.

steps.what: Supervisor evaluates the work bid from contractors and chooses one
Maintenance manager approves contracts above the spending limit
Buyer checks the final purchase order: contractor, scope, price and dates against the approved quote
Buyer issues the purchase order to the contractor
Supervisor coordinates permits, site access and safety with the contractor
Supervisor checks and accepts the completed work and signs the job order

tasks.design: A scope template filled from the job order and asset data in the maintenance management system ({OTHER}) is checked by the supervisor and sent once as a quote request to approved contractors from the {PROCUREMENT} system. A bounded step reads the returned quotes into one comparison table with source text and exclusions flagged; choosing, coordinating and accepting the work stay with the supervisor.
tasks.previous_blocker: Quotes in different layouts were copied by hand into spreadsheets.
tasks.enabler_now: Purchasing systems send requests for quotes, and language models extract fields from documents when each value must show its source.
tasks.still_hard: Comparing scope and quality is judgement; quotes with vague exclusions need a call.
tasks.human_edge: Spotting the contractor who underquoted and will come back for extras.

ambition.what: Three quotes compared for every contractor job, not only the large ones.

tasks.altitude: The supervisor compares a clean table instead of copying quotes; spending approval stays with the manager.

reach.learn: Whether the extraction step works on larger tenders.

evidence.claim: Purchasing systems send requests for quotes to approved suppliers.
An enterprise asset management system links maintenance work with ERP and supply chain.

assumptions: Boundary: from the scope of work to accepting the completed job; invoice payment is outside.
Input contract: asset data and job orders in the maintenance system; approved contractor list kept by purchasing; quotes returned by contractors as documents; fallback is copying by hand.
Manager, buyer and contractor time is outside the supervisor's savings.

Choosing, coordinating on site, acceptance, the request check and the send keep their full time. s1 keeps 70 because the template fills job and asset data and the supervisor writes the scope; s2 keeps 40 because contractors are picked from the approved list in one send; s3 keeps 50 for checking values and filling blanks.
unknowns: Number of contractor jobs per month.
Whether contractors reply in a standard format.
research_questions: How often does the exclusion flag find a scope gap?

already_counted.description: Supervisor checks the extracted table against the quotes.

incremental.description: Purchasing keeps the approved contractor list current.
No new upkeep for the supervisor: filling blanks left by the extraction is part of s3's remaining time.

approvals.approved_version: The purchase order with contractor, scope, price and dates exactly as checked by the buyer in s5b against the quote the manager approved in s5, sent once to the chosen contractor; any change in price or scope needs a new approval and check.
The quote request with scope, site and dates exactly as checked by the supervisor in s2c, sent once from the {PROCUREMENT} system to the contractors selected there; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: contractors send scanned or free-form quotes, so the extraction leaves many blanks and most values are still copied (13.6); high: quotes read with source text (18.6).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Collect work orders, enter hours, parts and findings, code failures, compile maintenance statistics and file test results.

steps.what: Mechanics close job orders on their phones with actual hours, parts used and notes
Supervisor collects completed work orders: on paper from the mechanics today; after the change only paper orders from mechanics without the app
Supervisor types hours, parts and findings into the maintenance system
Supervisor codes failure causes from the mechanics' notes

loop.input: The mechanic's free-text notes on a closed job order and the asset type.
loop.output: A proposed failure cause from the fixed list for that asset type, with the sentence it is based on.
loop.check: Code checks the cause is on the asset type's list and the quoted sentence appears in the notes. A second check asks whether the quoted sentence describes that cause; any code it does not support, every low-confidence case and every unlisted case go to the supervisor, who also samples a set share each week.
loop.stop: One pass per job order; unclear cases go to the supervisor.
loop.why_not_simpler: Mechanics describe failures in their own words; keyword rules mislabel them.

steps.what: Supervisor compiles maintenance statistics in a spreadsheet each month
Supervisor files test and inspection results for installations
Supervisor checks the month's figures: backlog, preventive share, repair time and downtime against what happened in the month
Supervisor releases the month's figures to the maintenance manager: by e-mail today, as one release of the dashboard month after the change
Maintenance manager reviews the monthly figures

tasks.design: Mechanics close job orders on their phones (paper stays for the few without the app) in the maintenance management system ({OTHER}) with hours, parts and notes, and a bounded step proposes a failure cause from the fixed list for the supervisor to sample. Backlog, preventive share, repair time and downtime per asset appear on a dashboard instead of a monthly spreadsheet; the supervisor checks the month and releases it once to the manager, and test results attach to the asset with their next due date.
tasks.previous_blocker: Work orders were paper and statistics were compiled by hand each month.
tasks.enabler_now: Maintenance systems take job orders from phones and show statistics; a documented case left spreadsheet follow-up and halved breakdowns.
tasks.still_hard: Data is only as good as the mechanics' entries; time records per mechanic need works council consent.
tasks.human_edge: Reading the numbers and knowing which ones point to a real problem on the floor.

ambition.what: Maintenance figures looked at weekly instead of once a month.

tasks.altitude: The supervisor checks and samples instead of typing and compiling.

reach.learn: Whether proposed failure codes are consistent enough for root-cause work.

evidence.claim: An enterprise asset management system offers downtime reporting by technicians and failure-mode strategies.
A Belgian lubricants plant cut breakdown time from about 300 to 115 hours a month and halved breakdowns after replacing partly spreadsheet-based follow-up (vendor case).
Time records per mechanic fall under works council consent for staff data and monitoring systems.
Asset dashboards are not high-risk AI; ranking mechanics with AI would be.

assumptions: Boundary: from closed work to monthly figures reviewed; maintenance planning is outside.

Input contract: hours, parts and notes entered by mechanics on job orders; failure cause list per asset type kept by the reliability engineer; test results from inspectors; fallback is paper work orders.
Statistics are per asset and team, not per mechanic.

Maintenance manager and mechanic time is outside the supervisor's savings; the mechanics' closing of job orders is step s0 (share 1, other role). s1 keeps 10 for paper orders that remain; s6 keeps 20 for the release; the month's check keeps its full time.
unknowns: Whether mechanics have phones or tablets on the floor.
How many job orders per month.
research_questions: How often does the supervisor change a proposed failure code?

already_counted.description: Supervisor reviews mechanics' entries on closed job orders.

incremental.description: Application manager keeps dashboards and the failure list working.

approvals.approved_version: The month's figures per asset and team exactly as checked by the supervisor in s6c, released once to the maintenance manager for the monthly review; any correction needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: mechanics leave many job orders incomplete or on paper, so the supervisor still collects and corrects much of the data (61.4); high: most job orders are closed complete on phones (73.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The maintenance supervisor keeps vendor talks, contractor choice and acceptance; compiling records, matching costs and copying quotes shrink.
role.ambitious_version: A supervisor who looks at maintenance figures weekly and compares three quotes for every contractor job.
